seo.title: Karmic tail 18 12 3 compatibility: the tower, the braid and the garden
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 12 3 compatibility — The Moon, The Hanged Man and The Empress: why a couple builds a secret world, lives by a thread and learns to come home.

title: Karmic tail 18-12-3 in compatibility: a tower that two people build together
short: No single person has the karmic tail 18-12-3: in a personal destiny matrix it cannot occur. It appears only when two people work out their compatibility, and with it The Devil takes the centre of the couple's chart — a card that neither partner has on their own. The three cards of this tail retell the story of Rapunzel. The Moon at the entry is the couple's shared wish for a secret world of their own. The Hanged Man in the middle is a union that hangs by a thread for years. The Empress is the main task: to come down from the tower and grow a garden of their own in daylight.

sections.h2: A tail that no single person has
paragraphs: The first clue lies in the numbers themselves. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail is worked out from two other points: entry M equals the main task D plus the centre. For the entry to be 18 when the task is 3, the centre would have to be 15. But no birth date ever gives a centre of 15: The Devil cannot stand in the centre of a personal matrix. So no individual has the tail 18-12-3.

A couple's points are counted differently: each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. And a run through every date shows something strange: the tail 18-12-3 forms in one way only. One partner always has the personal tail 3-7-22, the other 15-5-8. There are no other combinations. Add them point by point and this is what comes out:

ul: entry: one partner's Empress (3) plus the other's Devil (15) — **The Moon (18)**;
middle: The Chariot (7) plus The Hierophant (5) — **The Hanged Man (12)**;
main task: The Fool (22) plus Justice (8), 30 → **The Empress (3)**.

paragraphs: The personal tails also fix the personal centres: the tail 3-7-22 always comes with centre 8, Justice, and the tail 15-5-8 always with 7, The Chariot. Their sum is 15. That is why The Devil sits in the centre for 100% of couples with this tail.
Three observations follow from this arithmetic, and they hold for every such couple.

ol: **One partner's centre stands in the other's tail.** Justice, the centre of the partner with 3-7-22, is the main task of the personal tail 15-5-8. The Chariot, the centre of the partner with 15-5-8, is the middle of the tail 3-7-22. Where one feels at ease, the other has a lesson to learn.

**The entries of both tails do not vanish — they move.** The Empress, which opens the personal tail 3-7-22, becomes the couple's main task. The Devil, which opens 15-5-8, becomes the atmosphere inside the couple.
**Nobody brings The Devil into the centre.** It appears only between the two: Justice from one plus The Chariot from the other. The atmosphere of this couple is something they create together.

paragraphs: There is a fourth detail. If the middle were counted by the personal formula, from the two ends, it would be 18 + 3 = 21 — The World, completion and fullness. But the couple's middle is built from the partners' middles, and instead of The World it comes out as The Hanged Man. At the point where the road could have ended, it stalls.

The tail occurs in about one couple in 185 (0.539%) and ranks 52nd of the 97 couple tails. The rarity has a simple cause. The tail 15-5-8 is one of the most common personal tails — every eleventh birth date has it. But 3-7-22 belongs to only one date in 34.

sections.h2: A tale about a tower, rewritten for two hundred years
paragraphs: There is a story that begins with exactly this sum — The Empress and The Devil — and then runs through The Moon and The Hanged Man back to The Empress. It is "Rapunzel".

The tale has a long pedigree. In 1634 the Neapolitan Giambattista Basile published "Petrosinella": the heroine's name means "parsley". In 1698 the Frenchwoman Charlotte-Rose de Caumont de La Force brought out "Persinette" — again from the word for parsley, persil. In 1790 Friedrich Schulz retold it in German and swapped the parsley for rapunzel, a bellflower with a sweetish root that is eaten in salads. The Brothers Grimm took the tale from Schulz: in their collection it is number 12, and between the first edition of 1812 and the last of 1857 they rewrote it more than once. To the end the Grimms believed it was a folk tale — told "undoubtedly from oral tradition", as their notes put it in Margaret Hunt's 1884 English translation. Their notes say not a word about a French aristocrat's literary tale lying underneath.

The life of La Force herself is another clue. In 1687 she married a man six years younger than she was. The Church recognised the marriage, but her husband's father opposed it, and after two years in court the Parlement of Paris dissolved it. In 1697 the king sent her to the abbey of Gercy, and a year later her "Tales of Tales" came out, with "Persinette" among them. The girl who is loved in a tower without a door was invented by a woman whose husband's family would not let her have a home of her own.

The first page of the tale is that very sum of two personal tails. In the Grimms (quoted here and below in the same translation by Hunt) a small window at the back of a house looks into someone else's garden, "full of the most beautiful flowers and herbs", behind a high wall. A pregnant wife longs for the rampion in one of its beds. Her husband climbs over the wall twice, and both times at dusk — "in the twilight of evening", then "in the gloom of evening". The enchantress catches him and names her condition: he must give her the child. "It shall be well treated, and I will care for it like a mother." The garden and its plenty are The Empress. A bargain that speaks in the voice of care is The Devil. From the two of them comes a girl in a tower whom people visit only in the evening. For couples with 18-12-3, The Empress plus The Devil give The Moon at the entry. For the Grimms, that is how the tale begins.

And one more coincidence, too exact to pass over: "When she was twelve years old, the enchantress shut her into a tower, which lay in a forest, and had neither stairs nor door." In La Force the girl is already "a marvel" before she reaches her twelfth year — and that is when the fairy builds her a tower. The Hanged Man, the middle of this tail, is the twelfth arcanum. The tale knew nothing of the matrix, yet the number stands exactly where the suspended life begins.

sections.h2: The Moon: a shared language overheard from the gaoler
paragraphs: The prince does not look for Rapunzel — he hears her. Riding through the forest, he hears singing, looks for a door and finds none. Every day he comes back and listens from behind a tree until he learns the words that open the tower: "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, Let down thy hair." "If that is the ladder by which one mounts, I will for once try my fortune," he says, and the next day, "when it began to grow dark", he speaks the password himself. This couple's shared language is a set of words overheard from the gaoler.

La Force is even more precise. The prince "admirably counterfeited the Fairy's voice" (our translation from the French), and Persinette, "deceived by the sound of that voice", lets down her hair. Later the fairy pays him back in kind: she sings in Persinette's voice, and the prince climbs straight into the trap. Both enter the tower in someone else's voice. Even the light in Persinette's tower is not sunlight: the fairy built it of silver, the metal of the Moon in old alchemy, and its rooms are lit by the fire of carbuncles, "as bright as if the light of the sun had entered them".

This is what The Moon at the entry looks like. Point M is what the couple wants together — its agreements and its "shared language". With The Moon that language belongs to the night: pet names, jokes nobody else would get, understanding that needs no explaining, the feeling that together they know something about the world that others do not. Lisovskaya sees the bright side of this energy as high sensitivity, intuitive understanding and respect for each other's private space; here a partner is first of all a friend. But the tale's rule — "the old woman comes by day, you come in the evening" — has a price. The couple ends up with two lives: a daytime one for relatives, colleagues and acquaintances, and an evening one that is theirs. They take a long time to introduce each other to their families, each goes home to their own people for the holidays, and friends learn about the big events after the fact.

The Moon stands on the line of tasks, so its wish is also a form of resistance. In the tale the same password turns against the couple: the enchantress ties the cut braids to the window hook, and the familiar words bring down a trap. In everyday life it looks ordinary: something only the two of them knew becomes an argument in a quarrel — "you told me so yourself". Lisovskaya describes the shadow side of The Moon in a couple in just these terms: a partner's secrets become weapons, and jealousy grows out of stories that were made up. In Basile the secret is given away by the ogress's crony, "who was for ever prying into things that did not concern her" (John Edward Taylor's 1848 translation). Lisovskaya has this too: a Moon couple is secretive even at its best, and so it gathers rumours.

Benebell Wen writes that The Moon speaks of "the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time", and that "the repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing". In the tale the secret surfaces in a way that is both funny and frightening. In the first edition of 1812 Rapunzel innocently complains: "My little clothes are getting so tight" (our translation from the German). In the last, of 1857, she lets it slip: "Tell me, Dame Gothel, how it happens that you are so much heavier for me to draw up than the young King's son—he is with me in a moment." The scissors follow the slip at once — "snip, snap".

sections.h2: The Hanged Man: everything hangs by a hair
paragraphs: This couple's middle draws itself: in the tower everything hangs. The braids are wound round the window hook and fall twenty ells to the ground. The enchantress climbs them, and so does the prince. English would say a union like this hangs by a thread; Russian says it hangs na voloske — by a single hair. Here the hair is real.

In the edition of 1850 the Grimms added a scene that had not been there before. Rapunzel says to the prince: "I will willingly go away with thee, but I do not know how to get down. Bring with thee a skein of silk every time that thou comest, and I will weave a ladder with it, and when that is ready I will descend, and thou wilt take me on thy horse." Until then, they agreed, he would come every evening, "for the old woman came by day".

Readers have long asked why the prince did not simply bring a ladder. The tail answers the question: a ladder can be seen, but a skein of silk hides in a sleeve. The secret with which the couple entered the union also sets the speed of the way out of the tower — one thread per visit. The Hanged Man here is not a punishment but a way of life the couple chose for itself: everything is being prepared, nothing is being decided.

The arithmetic of the middle tells the same story. The couple's Hanged Man is built from the partners' middles — The Chariot (7) and The Hierophant (5). The tale has both. Below, a horse is waiting: The Chariot, readiness to break away and ride off. Above, a routine is in force — "the old woman by day, you in the evening": The Hierophant, an order the couple did not set up themselves. The wish to leave plus the habit of "this is how things are done here" add up to suspension.

Suspension can be happy, and that is its trap. In the 1812 edition the lovers in the tower "lived merrily and joyfully for a good while" (our translation). Lisovskaya's bright side of The Hanged Man in a couple is tact, attention, willingness to give way, the ability to sense each other at a distance. Yet she also makes an observation that reads like a summary of the tale: such couples are slow to enter a relationship, and they need a push from outside to marry. In the tale the push comes from a pair of scissors. In no edition of the Grimms is the ladder ever finished: the couple leaves the tower not by its own ladder but by a fall.

In real life the middle sounds familiar: "we'll move in together once we have a flat", "we'll tell our parents after the holidays", "we'll marry when everything is settled". Usually one partner holds the whole structure up — carries the silk, works out how to keep things hidden, how to fit everything in. In return they hear that everything is too slow, and by now they cannot leave. This too belongs to the shadow side of the twelfth energy in a couple: one partner holds the relationship together with all their strength, there are no shared goals, and nobody knows how to say no.

Wen compares The Hanged Man's sense of suspension to the question The Fool poses: "will the Seeker fall or fly?" The prince answers it literally — he leaps from the tower. "He escaped with his life, but the thorns into which he fell, pierced his eyes." For some years he wanders through the forest, eats "nothing but roots and berries", and finds Rapunzel not with his eyes but by her voice: "He heard a voice, and it seemed so familiar to him." It was by her voice, too, that he found her the first time.

sections.h2: The Empress: from someone else's garden to a kingdom of their own
paragraphs: The tale has two Empresses, and this is the tail's central secret. The first stands on the first page: someone else's garden behind a high wall, entered at dusk like a thief and paid for with a bargain. The second stands on the last: "He led her to his kingdom where he was joyfully received, and they lived for a long time afterwards, happy and contented." The main task of an 18-12-3 couple is to get from the first to the second: from plenty taken in secret and on credit to something of their own that needs no hiding.

In Basile the ogress, finding her parsley gone, swears to teach the thief a lesson and quotes a Neapolitan saying: "every one should eat off his own platter, and not meddle with other folks' cups". The ogress is the villain of the tale, but the saying is right, and it is almost word for word The Empress's task for this couple.

The most interesting thing is that the kingdom did not appear in the tale at once. The first edition of 1812 ends in the wilderness: Rapunzel's tears fall on the prince's eyes and he can see again — full stop. The line about the kingdom was added in the 1837 edition, the words "where he was joyfully received" by 1850, together with the silk ladder. The home in this tale took twenty-five years to build. It is the same for the couple: The Empress does not arrive on her own after a hard middle — she has to be written in.

Among the tasks of a couple with a three on this point, Lisovskaya names breaking free of the influence of a mother and relatives, swings of feast and famine, childishness and practicality. The tale has a scene for each of them.

The first is about family. The Grimms' enchantress promises to care for the child "like a mother", and it is exactly this motherly care that becomes the tower. In La Force the fairy softens at the end, arrives for the family in a gleaming chariot and drives them to the palace. But she seats herself "in the middle of these fortunate lovers". The picture is familiar: parents help with housing, money, grandchildren — and sit between the two. The Empress's task is not to refuse help but to change seats: nobody should sit between the partners.

The second is about money. Persinette's tower is bursting with riches: wardrobes as magnificent as those of the queens of Asia, jewels in every drawer, the most delicate dishes at every meal. In exile she has a hut of leaves by the sea and a basket of biscuits. On the very first evening after the reunion, a biscuit in the prince's hand turns to stone and the water turns to crystal. Plenty given by someone else's hand is taken away by the same hand: feast or famine in its purest form. What is truly the couple's own begins where the home and the income depend on the two of them, not on whoever is driving the chariot.

The third is about growing up. Rapunzel gives the secret away with a childish slip, the escape plan is meant to take years, the prince leaps from the tower in despair. Wen stresses that "the element of Earth governs this card". Everything that happens up high in the tale, in the air, on a braid, is a task of bringing it down to earth. In the tale the scissors do it: the cut braids "lay on the ground", the prince fell into thorns. The couple can come down by itself — by its own ladder.

The arithmetic of the main task says the same. The Fool (22), the task of one partner, plus Justice (8), the task of the other. The lightness of a leap and the sobriety of the scales, taken apart, give either a leap without looking or endless weighing. Together they give The Empress — a decision after which something begins to grow.

sections.h2: The Devil in the centre: "I thought I had separated thee from all the world"
paragraphs: When she learns the truth, the enchantress cries to Rapunzel: "I thought I had separated thee from all the world, and yet thou hast deceived me!" It is the most precise formula of The Devil in the whole tale: a love that wants to cut someone off from the world. The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what lies between the two and is not on show. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the fifteenth energy in a couple with a single thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

For an 18-12-3 couple it matters who builds the tower. The enchantress in the tale is a third party, but there is no third party in the numbers: The Devil in the centre is made from the partners' own centres, and neither of them has it alone. So the temptation of this couple is not someone else's ill will but their shared wish to become a tower for each other. "We don't need anyone", "we have our own world", "let nobody know" — that is how it sounds from inside, and at first it sounds like happiness.

At its best a centre of 15 means passion and a rare ability to accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes. At its worst it is that very "separated from all the world": jealousy of friends, of work, of the past, and attempts to hold on to a partner through intimacy, money, a shared roof. If the wish to possess turns into surveillance, prohibitions and threats, it is no longer a question of the tail but of safety: in that situation the thing to do is call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from a psychologist.

In a note of 1812 the Grimms warned that the shutting of a maiden in a tower occurs in many old songs — of Hildburg, of Brynhild — "and is therefore not exactly to be taken for a prison" (our translation). In the old songs a tower is not only a dungeon but also a shelter. A centre of 15 is not a verdict for this couple either: it is a shelter that becomes a prison once nobody keeps a door in it.

sections.h2: What Waite saw in these cards
paragraphs: The cards do not illustrate the tale. But Arthur Edward Waite, whose descriptions the classic deck was drawn from, left details that read like a commentary on it.

On Waite's Moon a road runs off to the horizon between two towers. He calls it "the issue into the unknown", and the dog and the wolf "the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit". Basile has a scene the Grimms lack. Petrosinella and the prince make a rope ladder themselves and climb down from the tower, and the ogress gives chase. Then the heroine throws three gallnuts onto the road, and up spring a Corsican bulldog, a lion and a wolf. At the very exit from the tower the same beasts appear that howl on the road between Waite's towers — only here they do not frighten the runaways but stop the pursuit. The fears at the exit work for those who have decided to leave.

Waite refused to call The Hanged Man a card of martyrdom: "the tree of sacrifice is living wood", "the face expresses deep entrancement, not suffering", and the figure as a whole "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". The prince who "escaped with his life" and the happy evenings in the tower both fit this formula.

On Waite's Devil, chains run from a ring in front of the altar to the necks of two figures, male and female. Waite calls this "the chain and fatality of the material life" and at once adds that he who is exalted above them "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". In the tale this is literal: every day the enchantress herself climbs the same braid. The keeper of the tower is tied to it no less than the one she keeps. In the same passage Waite calls The Devil "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit". "Rapunzel" begins with a forbidden garden bed.

And the sceptre of The Empress, Waite writes, "is surmounted by the globe of this world". The enchantress wanted to separate Rapunzel "from all the world"; The Empress holds that world in her hand. The couple's main task is to return to the world, not to hide from it.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a light in the tower window
paragraphs: The couple's spiritual purpose — on the site this is the sphere "The couple's values", the road the two are meant to walk together — comes in two kinds with this tail. For 73% of couples it is The Hermit (9), for 27% The Moon (18).

The Hermit among the values explains why the tower is so attractive in the first place. Rapunzel sings "in her solitude". La Force's Persinette "was never bored in her solitude: she read, she painted, she played instruments". Such a couple truly values quiet, depth and time of one's own: Lisovskaya, describing the nine at its best, writes that each partner has a time and a place to be alone, and that love is shown in deeds, not words. The task is not to give up solitude but to let it shine rather than lock the door. Waite says of The Hermit's light: "His beacon intimates that 'where I am, you also may be.'" In the tale that is how the song from the window sounds: it carries through the forest, and by the voice the prince finds Rapunzel — first at the tower, then in the wilderness.

If the couple's values are The Moon, night becomes not only the entry but also the shared road: the inner world, imagination, a pull towards the hidden. Then it matters all the more that this world has a door through which one can go out to people and come back.

The couple enters the union through a shared secret world — The Moon. To protect it, the important things are put off — The Hanged Man: silk is brought one skein at a time, and the ladder is never finished. No garden of their own appears, The Empress is left undone, and the couple lives on what belongs to others: help from relatives, temporary housing, an endless "later". Having nothing of their own tightens the attachment — The Devil in the centre: apart from each other they have nothing, and letting go is frightening. And the more frightening it is, the more tightly the tower is shut.

In La Force the fairy builds the tower out of fear: "since the Fairy knew her fate, she resolved to steal her away from her destinies". And once found out, she admits: "destinies cannot be avoided, and my foresight has been quite in vain". A tower built out of fear of life does not stop life — it only decides who will be in charge of it: the two of them or some outside force.

sections.h2: The way out: a tower needs a door
paragraphs: In the Grimms an outside force makes the exit for the couple: a slip of the tongue, scissors, a leap, years apart. In Basile, the oldest version, it is all different. The lovers make a rope ladder themselves, climb down themselves, fight off the pursuit themselves and reach the kingdom, where the prince takes Petrosinella to wife "with his father's free consent". The tail promises neither scenario. It shows where the couple can get ahead of the scissors:

ul: finish the ladder: name one concrete step — moving in together, meeting the families, a shared budget — and take it themselves, without waiting for circumstances to decide;
bring the shared language into the light: say to the "daytime" people — family and friends — what the two have agreed between themselves;
let nobody sit in the middle: accept help from elders in a way that leaves decisions with the couple;
test care for a leash: if "I take care of you" means "you can't go anywhere without me", it is no longer The Empress but The Devil;
never bring up in a quarrel what was entrusted between the two;
keep their night-time world, but not live in it alone: a home can have a window at the top as long as it also has a door at the bottom.

paragraphs: A strong 18-12-3 couple is the same two people who recognise each other's voice in the dark but no longer hide. Their Moon is a fine understanding without words and the ability to discover something new in the partner every year. Their Hanged Man is patience and the capacity to look at a situation from the other side. Their Empress is a home in which what they started together keeps growing. La Force ended "Persinette" with a moral in verse, and its last lines would do for this couple's motto: fortune is defied and fate overcome "as long as two spouses are of one accord" (tant que deux époux sont d'accord).
Take two dates: 05.12.1976 (5 December 1976) and 14.08.1975 (14 August 1975). First each person's personal matrix is worked out.

For the first date the day gives 5, the month 12, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Main task: 5 + 12 + 5 = 22. Centre: 5 + 12 + 5 + 22 = 44 → 8. Entry of the tail: 22 + 8 = 30 → 3, middle: 22 + 3 = 25 → 7. Personal tail — 3-7-22.

For the second date the day is 14, the month 8, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task: 14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8. Centre: 44 + 8 = 52 → 7. Entry: 8 + 7 = 15, middle: 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. Personal tail — 15-5-8.
Now the matching points are added together:
The couple's values in this example are The Hermit, 9.

This tail can be recognised without the whole matrix, from a single sum for each partner: the arcana of the day, month and year of birth. A day above 22 is reduced by adding its digits; the year arcanum is the sum of the year's digits, reduced to 22. For one partner the sum is exactly 22, for the other 26, 35, 44 or 53 — that is, above 22 and reducing to 8. In the example these are 5 + 12 + 5 = 22 and 14 + 8 + 22 = 44.

sections.h2: 18-12-3 and 18-3-12: the same cards in a different order
paragraphs: The same numbers form one more couple tail, 18-3-12. It is rarer (0.147% of couples), its centre is always The Lovers rather than The Devil, The Empress stands in the middle and The Hanged Man becomes the main task; its middle equals the reduced sum of the ends, and it also occurs as a personal tail.

ul: **Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together: a world hidden from other eyes, understanding without words, a private language that only the two of them speak. On the line of tasks the same wish also works as resistance: the secret makes it hard to step outside.

**Middle of the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** How the couple travels the road: in suspension. The relationship exists, but everything that matters — a home, a decision, a talk with the family — is put off until "the ladder is ready".

**Main task — 3, The Empress.** What the couple has to learn: to build its own life on solid ground — a home, a household, a shared plan — and not hand it over to anyone else: relatives, circumstances, chance.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-12-3 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, not a verdict. The entry is The Moon: a shared secret world and a language only the two of them understand. The middle is The Hanged Man: a union that lives in suspension for a long time and keeps putting off what matters. The main task is The Empress: their own home, their own household and their own decisions in daylight, with no one else's hand over the union.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With a task of 3 and an entry of 18, the centre would have to be 15, and no person ever has a centre of 15. A couple's points are sums of personal points, so 18-12-3 is possible for a couple — always as the sum of the personal tails 3-7-22 and 15-5-8.

faq.q: Is The Devil in the couple's centre a bad sign?
faq.a: No. It is an atmosphere of strong attachment. At its best it means passion and the ability to accept each other whole; at its worst, a wish to possess and jealousy. A centre of 15 appears only in a couple: two people create it, and the two of them decide whether their shared world will be a shelter or a tower without a door.

faq.q: How can a couple tell it has the tail 18-12-3 without working out the whole matrix?
faq.a: Add up the arcana of the day, month and year of birth for each partner. If one gets exactly 22 and the other 26, 35, 44 or 53, the couple has the tail 18-12-3. There is no other route to it: the partners' personal tails are always 3-7-22 and 15-5-8.

faq.q: Does this tail predict a separation or a hard fate for the couple?
faq.a: No. A karmic tail does not predict events, dates or outcomes. The tale shows the worst scenario, in which scissors and years apart make the way out of the tower. The cards show something else: where the couple can get ahead of that scenario and come down on its own.

faq.q: Which partner is Rapunzel and which is the prince?
faq.a: Neither. The roles of the tale are not divided by gender or between the partners. Both build the tower: The Devil in the centre is made from the centres of both, and the secret world belongs to both of them. Coming down from it is a task for both as well.

report: Readers of "Rapunzel" have long asked why the prince did not simply bring a ladder. For a couple with the tail 18-12-3 this child's question has a grown-up answer. The three cards of the tail — The Moon, The Hanged Man and The Empress — come in the same order as the tale: evening visits to a tower without a door, a life that hangs by a hair and, at last, a kingdom of their own.

report.h3: The tale begins with the same sum

report: No single person has this tail: 18-12-3 is born only between two. One partner's personal tail begins with The Empress, the other's with The Devil, and together they give The Moon at the entry. The first page of the Grimms' tale adds up the same way. A window looks into someone else's garden, "full of the most beautiful flowers and herbs", behind a high wall. A husband climbs in twice for the rampion "in the twilight of evening", and the enchantress names her condition: he must give her the child. "I will care for it like a mother." The garden is The Empress. A bargain that speaks in the voice of care is The Devil. Out of the two grows a girl in a tower whom people visit only in the evening.

report.h3: A shared language overheard from the gaoler

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its "shared language". With The Moon that language belongs to the night. The prince does not look for Rapunzel; he hears her singing, stands behind a tree and learns the words that open the tower: "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, Let down thy hair." In La Force's French version the prince "admirably counterfeited the Fairy's voice", and later the fairy sings in Persinette's voice and lures him into a trap. Both enter the tower in someone else's voice.

The couple lives the same way: pet names and private jokes, understanding without explanation, a feeling that together they know something about the world that others do not. And the tale's rule — the old woman by day, the beloved in the evening: a daytime life for relatives and acquaintances, an evening life that is theirs. But the same password can turn against the couple. The enchantress ties the cut braids to the window hook, and the familiar words bring down a trap. In everyday life it looks ordinary: something only the two of them knew becomes an argument in a quarrel.

report.h3: Why the ladder was never finished

report: The middle of the task is The Hanged Man, and in the tower everything really does hang: the enchantress climbs the braid, and so does the prince. The union hangs **by a single hair**. In the edition of 1850 the Grimms added Rapunzel's request: "Bring with thee a skein of silk every time that thou comest, and I will weave a ladder with it." A ladder can be seen; a skein of silk hides in a sleeve. The secret with which the couple entered the union also sets the speed of the way out: **one thread per visit**. Everything is being prepared, nothing is being decided: "we'll move in together once we have a flat", "we'll tell our parents after the holidays".

Suspension can be happy: in the first edition the lovers "lived merrily and joyfully for a good while". That is the trap. Lisovskaya observes that such couples need a push from outside to marry. In the tale the push comes from a pair of scissors. The ladder is never finished in any edition, and the tower is left not by the ladder but by a fall.

report.h3: Two gardens and someone sitting in the middle

report: The main task is The Empress, and the tale has two of them. The first is someone else's garden, entered like a thief and paid for with a bargain. The second is "his kingdom where he was joyfully received". The couple's task is **to get from someone else's garden to their own**, one that needs no hiding. The Grimms added the kingdom only in 1837, and the first edition ends in the wilderness. The home in this tale had to be built on later — and the couple, too, has to write it in for itself.

In La Force the fairy softens at the end and drives the family to the palace in her chariot, but she seats herself "in the middle of these fortunate lovers". The picture is familiar: elders help with housing and money — and sit between the two. Plenty given by someone else's hand is taken away by the same hand. The Empress's task is not to refuse help but to make sure nobody sits between the partners.

When she learns the truth, the enchantress cries: "I thought I had separated thee from all the world." This is the formula of The Devil, who stands in the centre of the couple, in its atmosphere. But the enchantress in the tale is a third party, and there is no third party in the numbers: The Devil appears only between the two. The temptation of this couple is **to become a tower for each other**: "we don't need anyone", "let nobody know". At its best this is passion and the ability to accept each other's dark sides; at its worst, jealousy and the wish to possess. Waite wrote of his Devil: "Even now, he is also a bondsman." In the tale the enchantress herself climbs the same braid every day. If the wish to possess turns into surveillance, prohibitions and threats, it becomes a matter of safety: the thing to do is call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from a psychologist.

In the oldest version of the tale, Basile's, the lovers made a rope ladder themselves and climbed down. The way out for a couple with this tail is the same: name one step — moving in together, meeting the families, a shared budget — and take it themselves; tell the "daytime" people what the two have agreed between themselves; never bring up in a quarrel what was entrusted; keep their night-time world, but **leave the tower a door**. La Force ended "Persinette" with a line that would do for this couple's motto: fate is overcome "as long as two spouses are of one accord".
